content.summary_of_the_paper: The manuscript handles the multi-label classification with noisy labels. To handle the problem, they propose the combinatorial correction (CCMLN), which incorporates both the instance-label dependence and label dependence to correct the noisy data, and thus help training the classifier.  Both theoretical and empirical results are provided to demonstrate the effectiveness of CCMLN.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Pros:
1) To prove the effectiveness of proposed method, the manuscript provides the theoretical and empirical analysis.
2) The authors sufficiently introduce the related works and employ a wide range of works for comparing. 
3) The improvement of the CCMLN in comparision with other methods are significant. 

Cons:
1) The proposed method assume that the number of true labels is the same with number of noisy labels for each sample, which significantly hurts its application in the real world, since the number of the labels with noise would be change with missing or redundant labels.

2) The main contribution of the manuscript is utilizing the label dependence learnt by the method introduced in [1] for correcting the noisy training data. However, its improvements are trivial according the corresponding results. Thus, the contribution of the paper seems to be limited.

3) Some details of the proposed method are omitted, e.g., when and how to get the y^{star} during the training is ambiguous, which hurts the reproducibility.

4) The authors could give the related results to prove the effectiveness of the proposed method for correcting the noisy data, e.g., quantitative results how many noisy labels are rectified.

[1] Zhao-Min Chen, Xiu-Shen Wei, Peng Wang, and Yanwen Guo. Multi-label image recognition with graph convolutional networks, CVPR, 2019.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
a) Clarity: The studied problem and proposed method are well presented and driven, along with sufficient introduction related works.

b) Quality: The proposed method significantly outperforms the compared methods.

c) Novelty: The idea of correcting the noisy data via label dependence for training are limited in novelty, due to it is widely employed in the partial multi label problem.

d)Reproducibility: The reproducibility of the proposed method is not strong, e.g., when and how to get the y^{star} during the training is ambiguous.

[1] Xie M K, Huang S J. Partial multi-label learning. AAAI, 2018.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper focus on the label noise problem in multiple-label scenario and consider tackling the label noise problem by the label dependence among multiple labels. Specifically, this article mainly answered three questions: why the label dependence is helpful for overcoming label noise problem, how to learn and utilize the label dependence into the label noise problem, and what improvements the label dependence can bring. On the basis of answering three questions, this paper proposes the CCMLN algorithm, and verifies the effectiveness of CCMLN by empirical evaluations. Besides, the additional use of label dependence brings higher probability to handle noisy multiple labels successfully than the sole use of instance-label dependence under some conditions, which is proved theoretically.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
This paper attempts to prove combinatorial scores better combat noisy labels in theory. And the experimental part is fulfilling, three types of baselines prove the effectiveness of the CCMLN algorithm from multiple aspects. The other experiments also analyzed the specific strategic details in the CCMLN algorithm.
Nevertheless, I think there are still the following problems to be solved. First, although the article has conducted various experiments, basically only the results are given, and there is not enough analysis of the experiment results. Besides, the paragraph of Section PRELIMINARIES "In many practical situations, it is easy to determine the number of objects in an image, in particular with object detection techniques. In contrast, it can be harder to annotate the objects perfectly, resulting in noisy labels.", when will this problem occur in the real scene, can the author give some more specific examples to illustrate the rationality of this setting? There are also some problems with typography. Most of the definitions of mathematics symbols are interspersed in text, not as formulas. This makes the papers, especially the "Proposed Method" section that look messy. The layout of some figures and tables of the experiment is also too crowded. Last but not least, this work is based on the method derived from the ADDGCN algorithm, but the improvement strategy used in this work is slightly simple and naive, and the innovation seems insufficient. Can the authors illustrate that the CCMLN algorithm should be better than the ADDGCN algorithm theoretically, or explain the innovation of the CCMLN algorithm more detailed from other perspectives?
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: This article has good originality and quality, as well as better clarity, but the clarity of the paper can be strengthened.

content.confidence: 2: You are willing to defend your assessment, but it is quite likely that you did not understand the central parts of the submission or that you are unfamiliar with some pieces of related work. Math/other details were not carefully checked.
content.summary_of_the_paper: In this work, a likelihood-test-like method is proposed to detect and correct potentially corrupted label assignments in multi-label learning tasks. The proposed method is designed specifically based on the multi-label classification method ADDGCN. It proposes to compute a likelihood score of a label assignment vector of a data point by combining the feature-label dependency and label-label dependency measurement. It then compares the ratio of the likelihood scores given the assigned label vector and the flipped label vector. Only If the likelihood ratio becomes less than a pre-specified threshold, the originally assigned label is preserved. Otherwise, the label vector is replaced by the flipped version. Experimental results confirm the validity of the proposed method.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strong point: 

It is an interesting idea to design the likelihood ration test to detect outliers in label assignments and correct the potential mislabelled samples. The idea is straightforward yet empirically effective. It explicitly explains how a label vector is considered as abnormal. 


Weakness: 
1. The implication of the theoretical study is not very clear. For example, what are potential value ranges of $C1$, $C2$, $\lambda_1$ and $\lambda_2$ ? How can we compute these values or estimate roughly the range of these values? Does the Tsybakov condition practically hold in multi-label learning tasks? 

2. The detection/correction method is designed based on the memorization effect of DNN models, i.e. easy training samples are well fitted before fitting the difficult samples. Therefore, the likelihood scores are computed before the ADDGCN model completely converges. However, difficult-to-learn samples are not necessarily mis-labelled. It is possible that filtering out the difficult samples using the likelihood ratio may cause overfitting the classifier to the easy samples. It is thus then an unanswered question how to choose a proper threshold for the likelihood ration and how to use at which stage of the training process we can count on the output from ADDGCN to filter the training samples. 

3. What is $\bar{y}_{new}$ in Eq.5 of Appendix B.1 ?
4. How to derive Eq.9 from Eq.8 in the proof of B.1 ?
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The paper is well organized and clearly convey the main contribution. It also provides enough details to reproduce the experimental results.
content.summary_of_the_review: Based on strong/weak points of this paper, I tend to recommend it as a marginal work. It is true that the empirical study looks solid and does confirm the effectiveness of the proposed method. The practical implication of the proposed method is not clear to me and difficult to understand how the theoretical justification can guide practical setting of the hyper-parameters in the proposed method. Besides, it is possible that a pre-matured DNN may miscategorise difficult but noise-free training samples as outliers and makes the proposed method exclude these genuine training instances by mistake. It is unclear how the proposed method may mitigate this issue in practices.

content.confidence: 4: You are confident in your assessment, but not absolutely certain. It is unlikely, but not impossible, that you did not understand some parts of the submission or that you are unfamiliar with some pieces of related work.
content.summary_of_the_paper: The authors introduce a new method for multi-label classification with noisy labels, in this case, noisy means that in the observed set of labels, the true label can be flipped to another label that is not already present, the number of labels in true set and observed set of labels is always the same. The method is an extension of an algorithm of Zheng et al., 2020 for multi-label settings. The core idea relies on the memorization effect in handling noisy labels - an observation that neural networks generalize well at the beginning of the training with noisy labels and only later do they start to memorize and overfit to noisy samples. Using such a classifier, in which training stopped earlier, the authors aim to correct the labeling of the samples in training set in a similar fashion as in the algorithm proposed by Zheng et al., 2020: correction of the labeling (prediction of early stopped classifier) is accepted if the "confidence" in the label correction being correct is larger than a selected threshold. The confidence is expressed as a ratio of combinatorial scores (introduced by the authors) of original, observed labeling and predicted labeling. The combinatorial score is a sum of marginal conditional probabilities of labels given instance and marginal conditional probabilities given instance and one other label in the labels set (considering all pairs). To estimate these probabilities and calculate combinatorial scores the early stopped model is used. The authors use ADDGCN (Ye et al., 2020) model, which is a graph neural network that can also be used to estimate marginal conditional probabilities of labels given instance and one other label in the labels set. The authors provide a theoretical guarantee on the success rate of the proposed method. Finally, the authors evaluate the proposed method on 3 popular benchmarks by generating noisy train sets by applying instance-independent noise to the clean train set. The proposed method outperforms the considered baselines.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:
+ The proposed method is a nice extension of an algorithm of Zheng et al., 2020 for multi-label settings.
+ The proposed method outperforms other algorithms considered in the comparison.
+ The additional experiments are nice additions.

Weaknesses/Questions
- It is not clear from the main paper why the authors used ADDGCN as a base of their solution. The answer is found in the appendix, that this method allows estimating $\mathbb{P}(l_i|l_j,\boldsymbol{x})$, which is needed to calculate an estimate of combinatorial scores. This should be better explained in the main paper.
- It is not entirely clear how the transition matrix works in this paper since $T_{ij} = \mathbb{P}(l_j \in \bar{\boldsymbol{y}} \land l_i \notin \bar{\boldsymbol{y}} | l_j \notin \boldsymbol{y} \land l_i \in \boldsymbol{y})$, the Appendindix describe both symmetrical and pariflip transition matrix $T$ with noise rate $\rho$, but it's presented in the way that suggests that there are no other labels in $\boldsymbol{y}$, so it is not entirely clear how dataset generation is handled in case of more than one label in $\boldsymbol{y}$ to avoid "collisions".
- How long is ADDGCN trained before being used as $h$ in Combinatorial Correction? I don't see this information.
- It is not clear to me how it is ensured that $\boldsymbol{y}^*$ has the same number of positive labels as $\bar{\boldsymbol{y}}$.
- The algorithm requires finding of threshold $\delta$, the authors in their experiments use a noisy validation set, but this seems to work only because the noise considered in the experiments is instance independent and uniform (almost, since I assume authors prevent label collisions). With instance-dependent noise finding the right threshold might be very difficult without a clean validation set.
- It also seems to me that the memorization effect might not be that strong when label noise is not longer instance independent.
- So far, it seems that the larger threshold $\delta$, the better performance, so why weren't the higher thresholds tested?
- The authors use the Tsybakov condition but do not cite the original work of Tsybakov et al.. 
- Also, in the introduction, when talking about applications of multi-label classification in different domains and noisy labels, the authors cite only very recent works, I believe these domains and noisy labels were also considered in older works that would be nice to cite. 
- The method is designed only for the specific type of noisy labels, the noise when labels are flipped to another label, I'm not sure if, indeed, it is so common to be certain about a number of objects, especially with problems of high granularity of labels, where objects might easily overlap. In the provided example, we could say that we are missing labels like: "life jacket", "water" or "waves".
- I also do not entirely agree with the authors' statements that it's not accurate to consider classification with missing labels as classification with noisy labels. Missing labels can be seen as one-sided noise and a special case of a more general setting than considered in the paper when any label can be either flipped from positive to negative or from negative to positive.

NITs:
- Figure 2 and 3 are almost impossible to read without 400% zoom. The document should be readable when printed.
- Some language suggestions:
  - label dependences -> label dependencies (I think this is more correct, in a few places)
  - (...) the deep model would firstly memorize (...) -> first
  - Definition 2 shares the similar idea and bound the uncertainty of S. -> bounds
  - Additionaly, (...) -> Additionally
  - We exploit pretrained ResNet-50 before. - I would remove before (or change the sentence in another way), it sounds strange in the present simple.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
Clarity and quality: Not all details are clear in the text, and some important parts are in the appendix.

Novelty: The proposed algorithm is an extension of the algorithm of Zheng et al., 2020 for multi-label settings, it seems to me that the novelty of this work comes mostly from the proposed combinatorial score that is formulated in the way that can be used with some architectures like used ADDGCN, what is not very novel but sufficient contribution.

Reproducibility: The paper contains some details on experimental protocol but not all the necessary details to guarantee the reproducibility of the results.
content.summary_of_the_review: I believe the manuscript requires some further work regarding the clarity of the presentation, many elements are not clear from the main text, and because of that, I'm leaning toward rejection.
